## Executive Summary


Physical AI brings intelligence into machines that sense, move, and act in the real world, creating new challenges beyond AI software alone.


- AI is becoming physical: Intelligence is moving into industrial equipment and robotic and autonomous systems.
- Hardware matters: Performance depends on integrating software with sophisticated physical systems.
- Scaling is a different challenge: Industrialization, manufacturing, and testing become critical beyond the prototype stage.
- Think across the lifecycle: Engineering and supply chain decisions can shape the path to commercialization.


Many people's first experiences with AI have been entirely digital: asking a chatbot a question, generating an image, or analyzing data. But a new phase of AI is taking shape in which intelligence doesn't just generate an answer; it senses, moves, and acts in the physical world.


This is physical AI. And as intelligence moves into robotic systems, autonomous systems, and industrial equipment, success will depend on more than AI software. It will require sophisticated hardware, engineering, infrastructure, supply chains, and the ability to scale complex physical products.


## What Is Physical AI?


Physical AI is the convergence of physical hardware with software intelligence, enabling a machine or device to interact intelligently with the physical world.


Traditional AI applications largely operate within digital environments. A user provides an input, an AI model processes it, and the system returns an output. Physical AI extends that intelligence into a physical object, such as an autonomous vehicle, drone, or industrial robot.


The important distinction is that AI is no longer limited to producing information. It becomes part of a physical system designed to sense, move, or act in real-world environments.


## How Is Physical AI Different from Generative AI?


Generative AI and physical AI describe different ways artificial intelligence is applied. Generative AI primarily creates or interprets digital content and information. Physical AI applies intelligence through hardware that operates in the physical world.


The two are not necessarily separate technology paths. Advances in AI software and the computing infrastructure that supports it are helping build the foundation for more capable physical systems. The key difference is where that intelligence ultimately operates.


## Where Is Physical AI Being Used?


Robotics is one of the clearest areas where physical AI is emerging, but the opportunity extends much further. Applications include autonomous vehicles and equipment, drones, industrial robotics, and intelligent industrial machines.


The potential also extends across medical technology, aerospace and defense, semiconductor capital equipment, and other complex technology markets. These applications share a growing convergence between sophisticated physical products and the intelligence needed to make them more capable.


This opportunity is emerging alongside advances in AI models, software, computing infrastructure, and semiconductor technologies. As those capabilities evolve, intelligence can move into a wider range of physical systems.


## Why Is Scaling Physical AI Challenging?


A physical AI product is ultimately a complex hardware system. Bringing one to market requires teams to solve how to industrialize, source, manufacture, test, and scale it.


Design decisions can affect manufacturability, cost, component availability, quality, and production scalability. For emerging physical AI companies, this can create a significant transition: developing an early product and building the systems required to commercialize it at scale are different challenges.


This is where an engineering-led approach becomes important. Celestica brings engineering and product realization together so that industrialization, Design for Excellence (DFX), Design for Manufacturing (DFM), Value Analysis/Value Engineering (VAVE), product development, and operational requirements can be considered as interconnected parts of the product lifecycle.


Supply-chain decisions are part of that equation. Component availability, logistics, regional requirements, and changing demand can influence how and where a product reaches the market. For emerging physical AI categories, where designs, volumes, and geographic requirements can change quickly, flexibility matters.


Celestica combines engineering expertise with local, regional, and global supply-chain and operational capabilities to create options as those requirements evolve. Rather than treating engineering, industrialization, supply chain, and production as disconnected stages, teams can address the product as an integrated system.


For companies developing physical AI, that integration can help create a clearer path from innovation to commercialization and scale.


## Physical AI Is Where Intelligence Meets the Real World


Physical AI expands the possibilities of artificial intelligence by giving intelligence a physical form. Robotics may be among its most visible applications today, but the transition is much broader.


As AI becomes integrated into more machines and systems, success will depend on connecting advances in software with equally sophisticated capabilities in hardware, engineering, industrialization, and supply chain. The challenge is turning that intelligence into physical products that can perform reliably and scale successfully.
